As January begins , many people are participating in Dry January . It 's an annual tradition where people take a monthlong break from drinking alcohol in order to reset their bodies and give their liver a much - needed break . It 's a popular trend , but it can also be hard for those who are participating . That 's why it 's [[important]] to be aware of what not to say to someone doing Dry January . 

 The number one thing to avoid saying is : " You do n't need to do Dry January , you do n't drink that much anyway . " It 's true that someone may not be a heavy drinker , but that does n't mean they do n't benefit from taking a month off from alcohol . Everyone 's body is different , and Dry January can help reset it and give it a break . So even if someone does n't drink heavily , they still may want to take part in Dry January . 

 Another thing to avoid saying is : " You should just cut down instead of completely giving it up . " Again , this statement overlooks the importance of taking a break from alcohol . People may not be able to control how much they drink when they are drinking , so taking a break is the best way for them to take back control . It 's also important to understand that for some people , cutting down is n't an option . Some individuals may have issues with alcohol that make it impossible for them to drink in moderation , so cutting down may not be an [[effective]] solution . 

 Next , one should avoid saying " It 's only a month , what 's the big deal ? " People who are doing Dry January should never be made to feel like their choice to take a break from alcohol is insignificant . It 's actually a big deal , and it 's a sign of commitment and strength to be able to go a month without drinking . 

 Also , it 's important to not say : " You 'll probably fail anyway . " This statement is incredibly discouraging and makes someone who is doing Dry January feel like they are doomed to fail before they even start . Instead , be supportive and encouraging . Remind them that it is possible to stick to their goal , and that they can do it . 

 Finally , it 's important to avoid saying : " You can still drink non - alcoholic beer , wine , and cocktails . " While these are great alternatives to traditional alcoholic beverages , they still contain a certain amount of alcohol and can still cause cravings . Instead , offer alternatives like seltzer water , soda water , sparkling juice , kombucha , and tea . 

 Overall , it 's important to be mindful of what you say to someone doing Dry January . While Dry January is n't for everyone , it 's [[important]] to respect those who choose to participate in it . Encourage them , be supportive , and offer helpful alternatives . Above all , remember that it takes a lot of strength and commitment to take a monthlong break from drinking alcohol , and that should never be downplayed .

Dear Abby : I was married for more than 40 years . My ex constantly badmouths me to everyone . He got to our grown daughter early during our separation , and it ’s clear to me she has sided with him . He ’s a very intelligent narcissist who manipulates people and they ’re not even aware of it . Our divorce took three [[different]] lawyers and cost me thousands , which was his intention . Should I open up to my daughter and try to get her to understand why I ca n’t be around him ? I do n’t want to alienate my only child . 

 — Free But Not Totally Happy 

 Dear Free : If you were married to your husband for 40 years , your daughter is no longer a child . Do not attempt to diminish her opinion of her father — simply explain why you could no longer stay married to him . If you can discuss your divorce with her and point out specific examples she may have noticed in her youth that led to your divorce , I see no reason why you should n’t . 

 Dear Abby : My daughter and I are both immunocompromised . I have cancer ; she has asthma and rheumatoid arthritis . Our doctors have advised us to not gather with crowds . We did n’t attend my nieces ’ wedding or her baby shower because nobody was masked and everyone was together . Now it seems like we have been forgotten . 

 We were not invited to recent holiday celebrations . My sister - in - law always sent group invites to these events , but we have n’t received any . They have n’t even asked us how we are . We are still not able to attend , but we would like to think we are still welcome . Am I justified in feeling this way ? 

 — Excluded in California 

 Dear Excluded : For the time being , you must accept that you wo n’t be able to mingle with large groups . However , that does n’t mean you ca n’t meet with small groups . To be less at risk , consider hosting some small get - togethers with vaccinated friends and relatives , and you may not feel so isolated . But please do not blame folks who know your circumstances , and whose invitations you have refused , for removing you from their guest lists for now .

In an unexpected corner of rural South Africa , a vibrant art scene is emerging from a long history of civil war and unrest . Hazyview , a small town in the east of the country , is home to an inspiring group of young artists who are creating huge tapestries that tell the story of their lives . 

 Since the end of apartheid in 1994 , Hazyview has gone through a transformation , with the introduction of art centers , schools and galleries . Young people in the town have had more access to the arts , which has helped them express themselves in powerful and meaningful ways . 

 The tapestry makers are a group of young artists , [[aged]] 18 to 30 , who work with a traditional weaving technique to create intricately - patterned works that depict the people and places of Hazyview . The tapestries tell the story of the town , from its past struggles to its current hopes for the future . 

 The tapestries range from small wall - hangings to huge wall murals . Some of the most popular designs feature traditional African patterns and images of wild animals , such as lions and zebras . Other designs feature stories from the local community and important moments from the town 's history . 

 The tapestries are made with a double - thread technique , in which two [[separate]] pieces of thread are woven together to create a unified whole . This process can take days or even weeks to complete , depending on the size and complexity of the design . 

 At the center of the project is Jacqui Thaker , a local artist and tutor . She has been helping the young people learn the traditional weaving technique and , crucially , discover their own unique style . She has encouraged them to find their own stories and put them into the tapestries – an idea that has captivated the artists and created a strong sense of collective identity . 

 The group has been collaborating with local institutions , such as schools and churches , to promote their work . They 've also had the opportunity to show their creations at art exhibitions in Europe . The international attention has been a source of great pride for the artists , and has raised awareness of Hazyview as a creative hub . 

 The tapestry makers have faced a few difficulties along the way , from the cost of buying the materials to the lack of resources in their town . However , Jacqui believes that the project has brought about positive change in Hazyview . " The tapestry makers have become a voice for the town , " she said .  Jan 4 ( Reuters ) - After winning a slim majority of seats in the U.S. House of Representatives in November 's midterm elections , Republicans are trying to elect a speaker . 

 WHAT IS THE SPEAKER 'S IMPORTANCE ? 

 The speaker of the House , [[second]] in the line of succession for the presidency after the vice president , leads the chamber and sets the legislative agenda and [[political]] tone . 

 Normally , the job goes to a lawmaker belonging to the party that controls the chamber with a majority of members , though it is possible for other people to be elected to the post , including an outsider who is not an elected lawmaker . 

 HOW IS THE SPEAKER CHOSEN ? 

 The [[full]] House of Representatives votes for the speaker on its first day of a new Congress , which was Tuesday . 

 A candidate must gain a majority of votes cast . With 435 seats in the chamber , the speaker must get 218 votes to win . If no candidate reaches that threshold , the House will continue voting until someone does . The record for longest vote was set in 1856 , when it took 133 ballots and two months to choose a speaker . 

 WHO IS THE SPEAKER NOW ? 

 Congress does not currently have a speaker . The House returned from its winter recess on Tuesday to elect a speaker and swear in newly elected representatives , but no one nominated received enough votes to win , despite three rounds of voting . It was the first time since 1923 that the speaker has n't been elected on the first ballot . 

 No other business - including swearing in new lawmakers and setting out the rules for House procedures - can take place until the speaker is chosen . 

 WHO IS THE LEADING CONTENDER TO BE THE NEXT SPEAKER ? 

 House Republican Leader Kevin McCarthy has long sought the job and was expected to finally achieve his goal on Tuesday , after dropping out of the race in 2015 due to opposition from hard - line conservative members . 

 But Tuesday turned into a recurring nightmare for McCarthy , as 20 far - right Republicans refused to support him in three back - to - back votes . He could afford only four " no " votes against his candidacy , given Republicans ' narrow margin of control and all Democrats voting against him . 

 WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ? 

 McCarthy and his allies are struggling to convince the hard liners to back him under any circumstances . He has already made major concessions to their demands , including lowering the threshold on the motion to vacate the chair , a procedural tool that would allow any member to trigger a vote of confidence in the speaker at any time . 

 However it 's not clear there is anything McCarthy could do to win over some of his detractors , given that they are not convinced he is committed to advancing their [[legislative]] goals . 

 WHO ARE THE POSSIBLE ALTERNATIVES ? 

 Republican Whip Steve Scalise , the No . 2 House Republican and a supporter of McCarthy , is a potential alternative whom moderates would vote for should McCarthy drop out . However some Republicans said on Tuesday that it did not make sense to drop McCarthy only to back someone ideologically and politically similar to him . 

 Representative Jim Jordan , a diehard conservative , got the support of all 20 anti - McCarthy Republicans on Tuesday , but vulnerable moderate members of his party would be unlikely to vote for him . Jordan himself nominated McCarthy on one of the ballots and repeatedly voted for him . 

 On Wednesday , those 20 conservative Republicans coalesced behind Representative Byron Donalds , one of the few Black members of the [[Republican]] conference and part of the [[right]] - wing bloc . Donalds is about to serve his second two - year term in Congress . 

 Democrats , meanwhile , have remained [[united]] behind their leader , Hakeem Jeffries , who unanimously won leadership of the House Democratic caucus in November .

Melissa Lyttle 

 In ELLE.com ’s monthly series Office Hours , we ask people in powerful positions to take us through their first jobs , worst jobs , and everything in between . This month , we spoke to Glennon Doyle , the best - selling , founder of the nonprofit Together Rising , and host of the podcast We Can Do Hard Things , named after her signature and oft - repeated motto . Doyle first started sharing her writing on her viral blog , Momastery , where she ’d open up about her life as a progressive Christian mother . Since those early internet days , Doyle ’s fans have watched her transform on and offline , all while navigating some of life ’s hardest — and most beautiful — things . Throughout her three memoirs , she ’s written about disordered eating and addiction ; motherhood ; infidelity ; divorce ; falling in love with her now - wife , the soccer legend Abby Wambach ; co - parenting ; and her ongoing mission to share her [[bravest]] and truest self with the world . “ When we are open and radically curious , we inevitably change , ” Doyle says . “ That , to me , is victory . ” Here , she shares how she ’s crafted her career as “ an anxious and highly - sensitive person , ” the intentional ways she protects her work , and the dream job she still has n’t done yet . 

 My first job 

 My first real job that was important to me was teaching . Both of my parents were teachers , and it was understood to be the most important job in the world . I still think that , and I still miss it . Little - known fact : The first book I ever published was a teaching book . My entire class spoke English as a second language , and [[most]] of my students were new immigrants . It was when No Child Left Behind was all the rage , and standardized testing was beginning to track kids in profoundly negative ways . I watched that happen to my students , because they were brilliant , but they were n’t able to show their brilliance on these tests . My colleague Amy Greene and I figured out a way to help them beat the tests that was legal . Our school started to use it , and then a bunch of schools in the district , and then it became a book called . Teaching is when I saw the effects of institutionalized racism and ableism and classism up close . I had a front row seat to it in a third grade classroom , watching my babies slowly be dismissed before they even got a chance . I think that affects everything that I do . 

 Doyle in August 2016 . The Washington Post // Getty Images 

 My worst job 

 I was a waitress for a while . In most jobs , there ’s a set of expectations that everyone agrees upon , and if you meet those expectations relatively , then you get paid , right ? With waitressing , that ’s not what happens . Every single freaking person that walks in has their own set of expectations for you and how you should behave and what means good service to them . A million times a night , you have to analyze other people ’s expectations of you and deliver , hoping to get paid . I do n’t know any other job that is so dependent upon the whims of any person that walks in for whether or not you make a living . 

 Melissa Lyttle 

 Why being a podcast host is perfect for me 

 I have always been a major introvert . I ’ve always said I love people , but not in person . I love humanity , but not human beings . As a super - sensitive , introverted kid , I would get to know people by sitting in a corner and reading over and over again . And that ’s what I do now . I basically do a [[sweeping]] book report on every person who comes on the pod . I go for walks , and I think about them , and my [ co - host ] sister and I come together , and we bounce ideas off of each other . Then [ my other co - host ] Abby responds to everything in real - time . I recently sent her this meme that said : “ Would n’t it be amazing to have the job of the podcast host whose only job is to respond in real - time to the other podcast hosts who ’ve been preparing ? ” But that ’s why people love her , because she ’s in the moment . 

 The best — and worst — part of working with my wife 

 Working with Abby means that our life is a continuous conversation . We do n’t have any separation between what ’s going on in our work life and in our [[personal]] conversations — and that ’s also the hard part . For example , I realized I was letting a frustration I was having with her on the podcast cross over . We were in a personal conversation , and I was so [[annoyed]] , because I felt like she was not being succinct enough . I was like , “ Wrap it up , wrap it up . ” Then we had to have a talk about how maybe we need to communicate more professionally in the podcast space so that I can say things like that there and not carry it over into the house . My point is that the hardest part is putting on two different hats . Here , we ’re colleagues , who also love each other and want to be tender with each other . Then when we ’re not on the podcast , I do n’t get to boss her around anymore . It ’s hard , but I feel so lucky . I would n’t have it any other way . And it ’s only hard because we ’re so careful with each other , because we love each other so much . 



 Melissa Lyttle 

 The intentional way I ’ve built my team 

 Throughout my career , I ’ve strategically kept my team very [[small]] . There have been a million turns in the road where we could have gotten bigger , but I knew I did n’t want that . I did n’t want to create a monster that I had to feed for the rest of my life . And as an artist and an activist , I needed to be with people who knew that I could blow this for us at any minute , even purposefully ; I could say something that would mean it was over . Everyone on my team knows that ’s how we live . We will never allow what ’s “ okay ” to say or do dictate whether or not we do it . That kind of nimbleness requires everyone to be so aligned and passionate about what we ’re doing . So our whole team is me , my sister , Abby , and our two best friends , Dynna and Allison . There ’s a [[positive]] side of keeping it so small , but the dark side is that everyone works too hard . We do n’t have great boundaries with each other , which is ironic , because we teach about boundaries . We are obsessed with boundaries ; it ’s just that we do n’t believe in them for ourselves [ laughs ] . So we are emailing and texting each other at two in the morning . But it works for us , because we are a teeny little family . 

 The way I view mental illness as a strength 

 I ’m constantly finding that the people I like the most — that I think are the most interesting , who are doing the most for the world , the most creative , the most kind , luminary people — are often people who have mental illness of some sort . A lot of people come to addiction because of that deep sensitivity or a yearning for something that is [[different]] than what is shown to us in everyday life . The distance between accepting everything for the way it is and yearning for more — though that can lead to quenching that with things that hurt us in the [[long]] run — is art , philanthropy , and activism . We can reach for things that hurt us , but when a lot of us figure that shit out , we still reach , and that reaching turns out to be everything that ’s good in the world . I think that people who are deep feelers or are anxious are often just people who are actually paying attention . If you ’re paying attention , there ’s a lot to be anxious about . Having said that , [ mental illness ] can be a doozy . 

 Doyle and Wambach in March 2022 . Charley Gallay // Getty Images 

 How I refocus after a stressful work day 

 I ’ll go for a walk with my wife . I think that walking saves me every day . I do n’t want to exercise anymore in a way that causes suffering ; I did enough of that in my life . And I do n’t put anything in my ears so that I can actually hear myself think . Then when I get home from that , I usually sit with my dogs . I just love my dogs so much . It ’s something about how they ’re the only beings who love me more the less productive I am . Everybody else , they say they love you , but they really want you to do shit . The dogs are like , “ Please , if you just sit here all day , if you just binge - watch Netflix , if you just stay here , we will love you more . ” 



 How I ’ve changed in the public eye while still honoring my past selves 

 I ’ve come to believe that life is about evolving . It ’s about constantly taking in every conversation , everything you read , every person you meet , every place you see , and allowing it to change you into the next , more beautiful version of yourself . And I do n’t think it has to be dramatic . When we are open and radically curious , we inevitably change . That , to me , is victory . But I ’ve come to understand that ’s not how everyone views life . People will say to me , “ How are you so different now than you were in your first book ? Are you being honest now , or were you being honest then ? ” But that was as true as I could be then , and now I ’m being as [[true]] as I can be now . If I was the same person I was 10 years ago , I would be devastated . I am constantly surprised by myself . Seven years ago , I thought I was a [[straight]] , Christian Pisces . Now , I ’m a queer , [[agnostic]] , [ and a little ] Christian - y Aries . I found out I ’m not even a freaking Pisces . I ’ve been reading the wrong horoscopes for 20 years ! And I wo n’t write another book until I ’m a [[new]] person . So I hope to keep changing .

 Fernando Báez Sosa estaba en una relación con Julieta Rossi , quien luego de la muerte del joven en un baile en el que ella también se encontraba habló con el medio argentino Infobae sobre su relación . 

 Era " mi compañero de aventuras , porque todo lo hacía con él " , contó entonces , recordando una vida compartida que incluía desde cantar karaoke hasta una clase de tango , y regalos que iban desde panqueques para su cumpleaños hasta una " pulsera de la distancia " [[para]] simbolizar su unión .

Llevaban , al momento de la muerte del joven , poco menos de un año de relación . Se espera que Rossi declare esta semana en el juicio .

 Instead , Silicon Valley will likely focus its attention on policies that both parties can agree on , like greater privacy protections and regulation of cryptocurrencies .

 Anthony Fauci , the leading U.S. infectious disease expert , said on Friday at the White House coronavirus task force briefing that while the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ( CDC ) is keeping a “ vigilant eye ” on the situation , the risk of the new variant spreading to the U.S. is “ quite low . ” 

 The variant , known as B.1.1.7 , was identified in the Chinese provinces of Yunnan and Sichuan . The variant , first found in China in October , is similar to that identified in the U.K. , and has prompted countries around the world to suspend travel from the U.K. 

 “ The report of this variant is obviously something to be taken seriously , ” Fauci said . “ We have a team at the CDC that is obviously looking into it and making decisions that are appropriate in terms of what they should and could do . ” 

 He added that there is no evidence yet that the new variant is more [[deadly]] than the original , though it may be more easily transmittable . He also noted that the variant has not been found in any countries outside of China . 

 “ At the moment , we are aware of it and it has not become a problem for us , and it will not become a problem for us unless it emerges in a country outside of the country in which it is originally located , ” Fauci said . 

 Fauci also emphasized the importance of wearing face masks and other measures to prevent the spread of Covid-19 . 

 “ We have been talking about the importance of not letting up on the public health measures that we know very well are effective against the standard virus and any variants that come about , ” Fauci said . 

 The news of the new variant comes as China is experiencing a resurgence in coronavirus cases . The country has recorded almost 4,000 new cases in the last two weeks , with the majority coming from the northern province of Heilongjiang , according to China ’s National Health Commission . 

 China has imposed travel restrictions and lockdowns in parts of Heilongjiang and [[other]] areas to slow the spread of the virus . It also has deployed Covid-19 testing teams to various parts of the country . 

 Fauci said the current measures China is taking to contain the virus are “ quite appropriate . ” 

 He also cautioned the public not to become complacent , noting that other countries are still seeing increases in Covid-19 cases and stressing the importance of continued safety measures , such as social distancing and mask wearing . 

 “ We 've got to keep our eye on the ball and continue to do the public health measures that we know very well are effective , ” Fauci said . 

 U.S. health officials have also been warning for weeks about new variants of the virus appearing in other countries . The U.K. has experienced a rapid spread of the B.1.1.7 variant , while the South African variant known as B.1.351 has been found in several countries , including the U.S. 

 CDC director Dr. Rochelle Walensky told reporters this week that B.1.1.7 had been detected in a small number of U.S. states . But she said the variants have not had a significant impact on the virus ’s spread in the U.S. 

 “ Right now , we believe the risk of these variants for widespread transmission in the United States is still quite low , ” Walensky said . 

 The [[new]] variant from China has increased concerns that the virus could be more easily spread and more difficult to contain . But Fauci said Friday that the risk to the U.S. remained “ quite low ” and that the CDC was continuing to monitor the situation .

Florida has been a haven for retirees for decades . From beachside condos in Boca Raton to seniors - only suburban developments like Century Village and The Villages , the Sunshine State 's endless summer and low cost of living attract thousands of elderly new residents each year . But rising home prices are threatening America 's retirement dream . 

 Median home values in Florida are up 33 % compared with last year , according to Zillow data , compared to a 18 % nationwide increase . The rising cost of Florida [[real]] estate is making things [[tough]] on people of all ages : Young people are delaying buying their first homes thanks to increased competition from private investors buying starter houses , renters are spending a larger share of their wages on housing , and some retirees are even going back to work to afford the roof over their head . After the Venetian Walk Senior Apartments in Venice , Florida , increased rents by $ 75 a month , several residents told the Sarasota Herald - Tribune that they 're worried they would n't be able to afford future rent hikes . 

 " If it keeps going up , we 'll just be treading water , " Art McLaughlin , a retiree who moved to Florida from Pennsylvania with his wife , told the paper . 

 Eight of the 10 most overvalued home markets in the country are in Florida , a study by researchers at Florida Atlantic University , Florida Gulf Coast University , and the University of Alabama found . 

 " It 's pretty well established that one of the state 's businesses — besides agriculture , hospitality , and real estate — is retirement communities , " Ken Johnson , a professor at Florida Atlantic University who focuses on real - estate markets and coauthored the study , told me . " The state is very much built around the retirement population moving to Florida . " 

 Between April 2020 and April 2021 , more than 300,000 people — not just retirees — moved to Florida , making it the top destination for people relocating states during the first year of the pandemic . The influx of residents , driven in part by the rise in remote work , has contributed to a rise in home prices . And retirees are feeling the squeeze . Housing prices , combined with the rise of remote work , threaten to end the middle - class dream of spending your final days in Florida . 

 Johnson said he did n't expect to see housing prices fall anytime soon . 

 " It does put the retirement industry at risk because it 's going to become more and more difficult " to retire in Florida , he told me . 

 ' California on the cheap ' 

 Florida 's status as a paradise for retirees was established more than 70 years ago , and it 's thrived as a place for Americans to spend their remaining days ever since . 

 " In the 20th century , Florida promoted itself as a poor man 's paradise : California on the [[cheap]] , " Gary Mormino , a professor of history and cofounder of the Florida studies program at the University of South Florida St. Petersburg , told me . " From 1945 to 2000 , one in four senior citizens who left another state in America moved to Florida ; no other state was even [[close]] . " 

 In the years following World War II , real - estate developers advertised Florida as an affordable paradise for people living off their newly established Social Security benefits . A book called " The Truth About Florida , " published in 1956 , promised that a couple could " live comfortably , have a whale of a [[good]] time , and save money " on just $ 40 a week — equivalent to about $ 440 today . Retirees developed enclaves based on where they previously lived : People from Detroit flocked to Lakeland , while southeastern Florida attracted [[older]] New Yorkers . 

 More than 4.5 million Floridians are 65 and over , meaning that more than one - fifth of the state 's population consists of people who are eligible for retirement — the second - highest percentage of [[older]] residents of any state in the country . Nationally , 16 % of Americans are 65 and over . 

 " In [[many]] ways , Florida is a modern twilight zone — a gerentopolis , " Mormino told me . 

 Florida has the second - [[highest]] percentage of residents over the age of 65 . That could change thanks to rising home prices . Eve Edelheit / The Washington Post / Getty Images 

 There are entire towns dedicated to the retirement - age population , some of which are populous enough to be census - designated places . One of the largest of these , The Villages , had nearly 80,000 residents in 2020 , up from 51,000 10 years earlier . A 2015 Pew study found that Sumter County , in central Florida , was the only county in the US where more than half the residents were of retirement age . Sumter is n't an anomaly ; 53 of Florida 's 67 counties have a [[disproportionate]] number of older people [[relative]] to the rest of the country , Pew found . 

 A new economic landscape 

 Florida has been long considered an affordable place to retire , an image communities across the state have sought to perpetuate . But if fewer people retire to Florida in years to come , the state may change considerably — both economically and politically . A study by the University of Florida found that older people contributed to the state 's tax revenues at roughly the same rate as other demographics but used far fewer state resources than , say , families with children . Florida retirees ' outsize influence on national politics is so well known that election year after election year , publications from across the country send reporters to The Villages to check its political pulse . 

 But rising home prices in Florida are already encouraging some retirees to look elsewhere . From 2016 to 2020 , the median price of owner - occupied homes in The Villages was just over $ 283,000 , according to census data . Today , the median - priced home in The Villages sells for $ 402,500 , according to updated data from the National Association of Realtors — a 42 % increase . A recent Bankrate analysis of July data found 17 states were more affordable to retire in than Florida . 

 Home prices are up about 20 % nationwide compared with this time last year , though markets like Florida are facing steeper increases than others . Peter Murphy , a cofounder of the Tampa , Florida , real - estate brokerage HomeProp , attributed the state 's rising housing costs to a combination of factors , including low supply of new or vacant homes , a growing population , and an influx of out - of - state homebuyers who can afford to spend more than their Floridian counterparts . A 2021 study by Zillow and Allied Van Lines found Sarasota was one of the top destinations for people moving to a new state and that the majority of people who relocated to Sarasota were from Chicago , New York City , and Washington , DC . Tampa was another major destination , with [[new]] residents primarily hailing from New York , Chicago , and Atlanta . [[Recent]] transplants told the Tampa Bay Times that they were drawn to the city because of its relatively affordable home prices compared with where they had come from , as well as the opportunity to work remotely . 

 " About 30 % of home sales are by all - cash buyers , " Murphy told me about the Florida real - estate market . Some are institutional investors who buy starter homes to convert them into single - family rentals . For example , in 2012 , the investment firm Blackstone bought hundreds of homes in the Tampa area that had been foreclosed on during the Great Recession to rent them out . A local real - estate broker working with Blackstone told the Tampa Bay Times that the firm was primarily interested in homes that cost between $ 100,000 and $ 175,000 . This year , Blackstone spent more than $ 300 million on 13 apartment complexes in Florida . 

 Not all cash buyers are investors . Retirees and well - off remote workers who sell their homes in other states can buy in Florida without having to take out a mortgage , especially if they 're coming from areas with higher home values . 

 The political influence of Florida retirees is so [[significant]] that national publications send reporters to The Villages before elections to check its political pulse . Joe Raedle / Getty Images 

 In the national market , " Florida remains a very good value for money , " Murphy told me , adding : " The median - priced home in the Florida market is around the high $ 300,000s to low $ 400,000s — so compared to what folks are coming out of in the Northeast , that 's a small fraction of what a similar home sells for there . " 

 Remote workers who flock to Florida from New York or Chicago have two advantages : They 're used to paying more for their homes , and they typically have higher salaries than Floridians . But people who have lived in Florida for a long time — including retirees — are finding it hard to compete with wealthier newcomers . 

 A rising tide that sinks some ships 

 Rising home prices wo n't affect all prospective retirees equally . " A lot of people approaching retirement own their homes , in which case rising home prices do n't really seem to affect their decision - making , " Geoffrey Sanzenbacher , a professor at Boston College and fellow at the university 's Center for Retirement Research , told me . " In some ways , rising home prices wo n't affect their retirement because their payment is fixed based on a past home price . " 

 People who are looking to sell their homes to relocate to Florida will still get more for their money than they would in more expensive states like California or New York , but they should expect to pay more now than they would 've a few years ago . For those who are already retired , rising property values are both a blessing and a curse . Retirees who own their homes may find themselves with more assets as a result of Florida 's rising home prices , but that also means they 're saddled with higher property taxes — an expense that may be hard for someone on a fixed income to afford . 

 " Maybe it 's attractive to New Yorkers , but it 's not as attractive to someone from Tennessee , Indiana , or Missouri , " Johnson , the Florida Atlantic University professor , said . Longtime Florida residents are also at a disadvantage — especially if they want to downsize or relocate to senior - only communities . " Relative to home prices and incomes , the typical Florida retiree wo n't be as well positioned to retire in Florida as , say , somebody coming from a more affluent area with higher incomes , " he added . 

 Even before the pandemic , some retirees found that Florida was n't the paradise they thought it would be . In 2019 , about 145,000 retirees moved to Florida , according to a study by SmartAsset , but an estimated 78,500 older people left the state that same year . A growing number of Floridians — including some who previously moved there from other states — are relocating to places like North Carolina , where more than 425,000 Floridians moved between 2006 and 2019 . 

 The dream of a Florida retirement is dying as housing prices make it too expensive for most . Joe Raedle / Getty Images 

 Alfred Ortwein , a 79 - year - old who lives in a suburb of Tampa with his wife , recently told the Tampa Bay Times that he knew several retirees who abandoned the idea of retiring in Florida . " My friends back in Delaware are considering Alabama and Tennessee — they are n't looking at Florida , " he said . " If I were looking to retire now , I could n't move here . I 'm sure there are places that are still more livable , but they 're not in the Tampa area . " 

 Ortwein and his wife own their home , so their mortgage payments have n't changed — but rising home values in the Tampa area have affected them anyway . Their home value doubled , the couple said , but that means they have a higher property - tax bill . 

 Unless Florida builds more housing and raises wages , Johnson foresees that housing prices will keep rising — and that Floridians , including those of retirement age , will continue to be priced out by transplants and snowbirds . " We are n't going to see a crash , but we 'll have very unaffordable housing relative to our incomes , " he said . 

 And if the trend continues , rising home prices may delay young people 's retirement plans . Most older people own their homes , Sanzenbacher said , but homeownership rates for millennials are lagging . More than 90 % of baby boomers were homeowners at some point between 1980 and 2016 , according to Statista . One 2019 study found that 76 % of boomers were homeowners . Meanwhile , less than half of all millennials owned their homes in 2020 . Even those millennials who do manage to buy homes are at a disadvantage compared with members of previous generations . 

 " If you have a 30 - year mortgage , and you do n't buy your first house until you 're 40 , that means you 'll still have a mortgage until you 're 70 , " Sanzenbacher said . " If you have a mortgage , it 's going to be a lot harder to retire . The longer people delay buying a home and getting that mortgage , the longer until they can retire free and clear of it . " 

 For young people , the idea of retiring anywhere may be out of reach , or at least delayed . And for people who are retiring now , the Florida retirement dream is starting to look a lot less sunny . 

 Gaby Del Valle is a writer and reporter living in Brooklyn .

 The world of soccer was rocked on Tuesday after news broke that [[Brazilian]] soccer legend Pelé had passed away at the age of 82 . 

 Pelé , who retired from professional soccer in 1977 , was widely considered one of the [[greatest]] players of all time . He won three World Cup titles with the [[Brazilian]] national team , scoring six goals in two finals . 

 He was one of the few soccer stars whose name was known around the world , and he was a cultural icon in Brazil , where he was born Edson Arantes do Nascimento . 

 Pelé 's death was announced in a statement released by the Brazilian Football Confederation ( CBF ) . 

 " The Brazilian Football Confederation deeply regrets the death of Edson Arantes do Nascimento , Pelé , " the statement said . " The King of Football left us today after a life dedicated to spreading joy and the love of sport . 

 " Edson Arantes do Nascimento became Pelé when he started playing professionally in Santos FC , and his legacy reaches far beyond football . " 

 Pelé 's life began humbly in Tres Coracoes , Brazil , where he grew up in a poor family with 10 siblings . He showed his talent early and was signed by Santos FC at the age of 15 , becoming an instant star in the club . 

 He scored an incredible 177 goals in 172 appearances for Santos , and in the process , helped them to multiple titles , including an incredible five [[consecutive]] Campeonato Paulista championships . 

 Pelé also made a name for himself with the Brazilian national team , helping them to their first World Cup title in 1958 , and then two more in 1962 and 1970 . His record of 12 goals in 14 World Cup matches still stands today , and he was the first player to score in three different tournaments . 

 Off the pitch , Pelé made a name for himself through endorsements , which included Coca - Cola , Honda , and the United Nations , among others . 

 He was also active in the fight against racism , HIV / AIDS , and child labor , and was awarded the World Cup Golden Boot in 2000 , the FIFA World Player of the Century award in 1999 , the International Peace Award in 1978 , and the UN ’s Person of the Year Award in 1995 , among other honors . 

 Pelé also received the Knight of the French Legion of Honor in 1998 , and was granted honorary citizenship in his home country of Brazil . 

 In the wake of his death , tributes have come pouring in from fellow soccer stars and world leaders . 

 " Sad to hear the news of the passing of my childhood hero , a real football God , " tweeted Brazilian superstar Neymar . 

 " Football has lost a legend , and we are all poorer for his passing , " tweeted Diego Maradona , another soccer great . 

 FIFA president Gianni Infantino also paid his respects . 

 " His legacy will continue to inspire millions of football fans around the world , " he said . 

 Pelé is survived by his wife and three children . He will forever be remembered as one of the greatest soccer players in history , and his legacy will live on in the hearts and minds of those who love the game .

Both events , The Global Times argued , are reminders of just how fragile the [[American]] democratic experiment remains , and why , in critics ’ eyes , it might n’t be the shining example its defenders suggest . 

 “ Faced with the political chaos in the U.S. , there is a sharp question whether the political class of the country is [[able]] to govern , and whether the internal conflicts and contradictions of one of the major political parties contaminate the entire system , ” editors there wrote , helpfully in English , slagging the [[ongoing]] drama that has since entered its fourth day of balloting . 

 Put simply : the American system is problematic and maybe best avoided . 

 The diagnosis stings a bit more after a week like this one , although the comparison between a House procedural vote and an insurrection is as messy as democracy itself . The timing is sure to trigger those of us who are watching the evolution of both stories , one after four days and the other after two years . One stubborn , the other violent , the two events laced together twin narratives about democracy itself , one in which elected officials get to cast votes and the other in which votes themselves can be ignored . But at the 30,000 - foot level , each moment deserves some introspection . 

 And yet this is the state of Washington — and U.S. democracy — as 2023 starts , sending up plenty of worries for what the next two years of government stand to be . Republicans have a majority in the House but ca n’t even settle on one person to lead them . Now , 13 failed ballots deep into McCarthy ’s maybe - quixotic climb to the Speaker role , Washington is trying to figure out what parts of the House might be salvaged and what others might just need to head to the scrap yard until , at least , 2024 . 

 The typically pro forma effort to select a Speaker began on Tuesday and may stretch through the weekend . That the first vote did n’t yield a choice for a role that is only behind the Vice President in the constitutional line of succession for the Oval Office for the first time in a century should freak people out . The fact that there has been so dramatically little movement four days later should tee up panic . 

 Which is why the world well beyond the Beltway has noticed the mess — especially in capitals of the United States ’ biggest foes , rivals , and adversaries . Facts do n’t stop at borders the way they did during the glory of the Cold War . 

 After Wednesday ’s votes foretold a protracted battle , military veterans now armed with voting cards invited reporters to a briefing room off the House floor to explain the global stakes of what their colleagues were doing . 

 “ Authoritarian regimes all over the world are pointing to what is going on in the House of Representatives and saying Look at the messiness of democracy , look at how it does n’t work , how it ca n’t function — and in contrast to their authoritarian regimes , ” Rep. Michael Waltz , R - Fla. , told reporters . ( Of course , they were all urging colleagues to drop opposition to McCarthy and fall in line in the name of Uncle Sam . ) 

 Waltz was n’t wrong . The propaganda arms of North Korea , Iran , Venezuela , Cuba , and Russia all highlighted the unusual instability unfolding on the Hill . In many of the same stories , they noted that jostling overlapped with the anniversary of the 2021 riot , which sought to destabilize the electoral system , too . Imperfect comparisons , for sure , given one was an intra - [[party]] feud and the other a violent attempt to circumvent democracy itself , but nonetheless proof points of America ’s imperfections . 

 The tactic is hardly new . During the Civil Rights Movement and beyond , Soviet propagandists accurately reported on the lynching of Blacks in the South as evidence of America ’s incomplete promises of equality . Vietnam was a propagandist ’s bonanza for critics of the United States and the West . The post–9/11 War on Terror offered no shortage of hypocrisy , especially when it came to Gitmo and contradictions about the so - called [[American]] leadership in the world . And recent Black Lives Matter protests were made - for - Pravda moments highlighting once again the incomplete promise of American democracy . Lower in the stories , the critics could toss in some ad hominem attacks on Washington , buttressed by the facts that America was already proven a troubled preacher of its values . 

 All of which is to say this : the mess at the Capitol certainly does not put America ’s best foot forward when it comes to propaganda . It ’s an embarrassment on a global stage that this is dragging on in such a purely tribal way and the facts need no embellishment . But , on its own , the delay in picking a Speaker does n’t mean the system is broken . It just means the people running it might have substituted their personal ambitions for realism . The sin is n’t the system ; it ’s hubris . Few Americans will notice the Communist tabloid ’s verdict on the tableau in Washington , but it will inform Chinese minds far more than anything published in Western outlets . It might be time for lawmakers to look inward and see what they ’re doing , not just to themselves and their party , but to America ’s image abroad .

A collection of rare and unseen photographs from 1950s Japan has offered an insight into the country 's seemingly rapid modernization during a period of rapid [[economic]] growth . 

 The photographs , taken by the [[late]] Japanese photographer Nagasaki Kenichi , are part of an exhibition at the Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography , which runs until the end of the month . 

 During the 1950s , Japan experienced a period of unprecedented growth , known as the " economic miracle , " as its GDP rose by an average of 10 percent a year . 

 The development was made [[possible]] in part by the country 's high savings rate , which rose from 22.2 percent of GDP in 1953 to 44.8 percent in 1960 . 

 With people putting more money away , and the government pouring funds into infrastructure and economic stimulation , Japan was [[able]] to grow into one of the world 's major industrial powers in little over a decade . 

 Kenichi 's photographs , taken during a three - year journey through Japan between 1955 and 1958 , show the country during this period of extraordinary change . 

 In the city of Yokohama , the photographer captured images of a bustling port and of life in the newly - constructed postwar housing blocks . 

 The former , Kenichi wrote , had become " a gateway to the world , with its modern port , subway , and technological developments . " The latter , he said , depicted " a life of hope and struggle in Japan 's postwar housing . " 

 Elsewhere in his native country , Kenichi turned his lens to Japan 's labor movement , capturing images of [[unionized]] workers as they took part in strikes and demonstrations . 

 Frequently viewed as a less glamorous counterpart to Japan 's economic boom , these photographs bring to life the plight of workers often treated as second - class citizens amid the country 's rapid industrialization . 

 One photograph from the industrial town of Shizuoka shows a crowd of workers holding a banner that reads " make sure all workers can share the fruits of our labor . " 

 Throughout his travels , Kenichi sought to document the ordinary lives of ordinary people during Japan 's postwar transformation . His work , said Tokyo museum curator Yorinobu Noda , " tells the story of Japan 's modernization from the perspective of the people living in it . " 

 " In showing Japan 's growth at the same time that it reveals the individual stories of those left behind , " Noda added , " we can gain a more nuanced understanding of the country 's experience at that time . " 

 Though Kenichi died in 1984 , his pictures offer a unique window into a transformative period of modern history . Whether photographed in the factories and fishing villages of western Japan or the bustling cityscapes of Tokyo and Yokohama , his pictures reveal an often unseen side of an otherwise booming economy . 

 It 's a reminder that while Japan 's economic miracle saw the nation become a major global power in a relatively [[short]] space of time , those in its working class still experienced difficult lives , often with the [[same]] struggles still seen today .

The Environmental Protection Agency and Army Corps of Engineers on Friday announced a new definition of " waters of the United States , " a classification that has been debated for decades . 

 At issue is which types of waterways — wetlands , rivers , lakes , etc . — are protected under the Clean Water Act , which was signed into law 50 years ago . The act regulates water pollutants and empowers the EPA and the Army Corps of Engineers to define which particular bodies of water are protected by law . Protected bodies of water [[qualify]] for federal programs pertaining to oil spill prevention , water quality regulation and more . 

 During the Obama administration in 2015 , the EPA established a relatively broad definition of waters of the United States , or WOTUS , that included navigable waters such as the Mississippi River and the Pacific and Atlantic oceans , as well as rivers , lakes and wetlands that crossed state borders . But in 2020 , the Trump administration limited the types of waterways that received the federal protections , excluding much of the country ’s wetlands and smaller waterways . 

 The new definition announced this week instates similar protections to those that were in place before 2015 , while also clarifying certain qualifications for protected waters . 

 Like the 2015 rules , navigable waters , oceans , and interstate waterways are protected by default . Tributaries that flow into and affect larger bodies of water , as well as wetlands near protected waters and some additional lakes and ponds can also be protected . To qualify , such smaller waterways must meet a set of standards that focuses on their permanence and their interconnectedness with other bodies of water . These updated standards are , in part , a response to several Supreme Court decisions in cases that challenged past definitions of WOTUS over the last two decades . 

 In a news release , the EPA said the new rule is intended to " reduce uncertainty from changing [[regulatory]] definitions , protect people ’s health , and support economic opportunity . " 

 " What we are doing with this final rule is establishing a clear and reasonable definition of waters of the United States , " Radhika Fox , the assistant administrator for the EPA ’s Office of Water , told NBC News . 

 She added , " We set water quality standards for lakes and streams all around the country , and that is what makes sure that if you ’re eating out of that lake and if you ’re swimming in that stream that it ’s safe for you . " 

 The new rule also establishes some exclusions from WOTUS : wetlands that were converted to cropland before 1985 , waste treatment centers , ditches , areas with human - made irrigation , artificial lakes and ponds , and artificial pools . 

 " This comes at a time when we ’re seeing unprecedented attacks on federal clean water protections by polluters and their allies , " said Jon Devine , director of federal water policy for the Natural Resources Defense Council . " While the nation still has significant work to do to fully protect important waters , it ’s encouraging to see the country taking a step in the right direction to protect the waters we need for everyone ’s health and the environment . " 

 However , [[Republican]] Sen. Shelley Moore Capito , a member of the Environment and Public Works Committee , voiced her opposition to the new rule . 

 " Reform is badly needed for infrastructure , transportation , and energy projects of all kinds to move forward . Unfortunately , this rule would move us backwards by making more projects subject to federal permitting requirements and adding more bureaucratic red tape , " Capito said in a statement . 

 The Supreme Court is set to issue a decision next year in a case challenging the EPA ’s determination that a wetland on [[private]] land in Idaho is protected under the Clean Water Act . That decision could impact future rules about WOTUS . 

 Changes to the definition of WOTUS during past presidential administrations have commonly given rise to lawsuits .

 January 8th , 2023 marked a special day for countless women around the world : It was the day of the long - awaited announcement by the World Health Organization that a [[new]] option for women seeking infertility treatments was [[available]] . The procedure , known as “ Gestational Carrying ” , was the first of its kind and was made available to all women who were [[unable]] to conceive or carry a child of their own . 

 The idea of Gestational Carrying came out of the partnership between WHO , the International Planned Parenthood Federation , and the United Nations Population Fund . The idea was to give women an option for pregnancy and childbirth that did not rely on the traditional IVF process . Gestational Carrying uses a [[third]] - party surrogate who carries the baby to term for the woman in need . This option allows women to experience the joy and connection of motherhood without having to undergo the invasive , [[expensive]] , and often unsuccessful procedures of IVF treatments . 

 The process is a simple one . After an [[initial]] consultation with a doctor , a woman looking to participate in Gestational Carrying would be matched with an [[appropriate]] surrogate who is willing and able to carry the child to term . Once the surrogate has been determined , a detailed contract is established between the surrogate and intended mother . This agreement specifies various details such as medical care , living expenses , legal rights , and compensation . 

 Although there is still much to learn about the gestational carrying process , the early reactions to the procedure have been overwhelmingly positive . For example , one user on Twitter proclaimed , “ I ’ve wanted to become a mother for years but I just could n’t make it happen for me . With this new option , I ’m one step closer to making my dream come true . ” 

 Gestational Carrying offers a range of potential benefits to women in need of fertility treatments . For starters , the process is significantly less expensive and invasive than traditional IVF treatments . Additionally , this new option allows the intended mother to establish a deeper bond with her surrogate and her unborn child , as the surrogate would carry the baby to term on behalf of the mother . This can be incredibly beneficial for those who are struggling with the idea of not being able to carry their own child . 

 While Gestational Carrying is still a relatively [[new]] option , it offers many women a chance to experience motherhood in a way they may not have been able to before . Whether a woman is struggling with infertility , facing other [[medical]] challenges , or simply prefers not to conceive in the traditional way , Gestational Carrying has opened up a new avenue for them to potentially become mothers . Ultimately , Gestational Carrying is a revolutionary step forward for those who wish to experience the joy of parenthood and the loving bond between mother and child .

 NVIDIA DRIVE Thor , the company 's next - generation centralized computer for autonomous and assisted driving and in - car infotainment , is shown in a handout image obtained September 20 , 2022 .

At the start of a two - day trip to the United States - Mexico border , President Joe Biden on Wednesday said he 's frustrated with [[Republican]] lawmakers who he says have not been [[serious]] about addressing the country 's immigration system . 

 Biden made the comments during an interview with CNN as he prepared to travel to Texas , his first trip to the border since taking office . He said that despite his administration 's efforts to address the country 's immigration system , Republicans have not been willing to take any meaningful action to move the issue forward . 

 " I 'm frustrated that Republicans have n't been serious about this at all , " Biden said . " They 've never been [[serious]] about it . We 've been trying to get Republicans to the table since the beginning of my term . " 

 The president 's remarks come at a time when the White House and lawmakers are engaged in intense negotiations over an immigration reform package . The administration has signaled that it is willing to accept a " soft " version of the Dream and Promise Act , which provides a pathway to citizenship for immigrants who arrived in the United States as children and those with [[temporary]] protected status or have been granted deferred action under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals ( DACA ) program . 

 However , Republicans have been largely critical of the White House 's plans and the Democrats ' proposed legislation , arguing that the proposed pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants is an amnesty for those who have come to the U.S. illegally . 

 Biden expressed optimism that progress can be made on the issue , but said the key is to ensure that any legislation is " carefully crafted " and " does not make any major changes to the basic structure of our immigration system . " 

 " We have to have a policy in place to make [[sure]] that if somebody comes in , they 're not just given an open - door policy , " Biden said . " They have to be able to be vetted and make sure that we 're not allowing people who could be a threat to the country in . " 

 Biden is also set to meet with local officials , faith leaders and other stakeholders in El Paso , Texas on Wednesday and Thursday to discuss the administration 's efforts to tackle the surge of unaccompanied minors and families at the border . The White House has said that Biden will provide an update on its ongoing efforts to strengthen the border and ensure the safety of children and their families . 

 The president is expected to emphasize the administration 's actions to ensure safe , orderly , and humane migration while also calling on Congress to pass [[comprehensive]] immigration reform . 

 In the meantime , Biden has been urging Congress to pass legislation providing additional assistance to the Central American nations of El Salvador , Guatemala , and Honduras , in order to help address the root causes of migration . He also said in his interview that he wanted to take a closer look at the Migrant Protection Protocols , the controversial policy enacted by former President Donald Trump 's administration that required asylum - seekers to remain in Mexico while awaiting a ruling . 

 " We 're going to have to be careful in how we unravel this , " Biden said . " But that does n't mean we 're not going to move in a very , very rapid fashion to try to get this on the right track . " 

 Biden also expressed optimism about the prospects for comprehensive immigration reform , saying , " I believe it is possible to get something done . " 

 " We ca n't just keep going on with the status quo and leave the border open and people to come in , " he said . " We have to do something about it . " 

 At the same time , the president warned Republicans against using the issue for political gain , saying , " I think that 's one of the greatest dangers right now ... I'm going to work in a bipartisan way to get this solved . But if we do n't , I 'm prepared to act unilaterally , in a very , very significant way . "

Getting acquired by a bank might seem like a dream scenario for a fintech founder . But at one West Coast digital - payments startup , it quickly became a nightmare . 

 The ink had barely dried on the deal when cultural issues started to arise between bank leadership and the startup 's executives , said Robert Ruark , a principal at KPMG , a consultancy that worked with the bank on the acquisition . 

 The fintech team found the pace of business at the bank painfully slow and its regulatory burdens heavy , Ruark said . Even the meeting schedule ( [[complete]] with " inordinate time " spent on " introductions and pleasantries , " Ruark said ) became a point of contention , as the startup execs complained they did n't have time to get any work done . 

 Things came to a head after the fintech founder 's digital - payments expansion plan was nixed — the latest in a series of projects that had been uniformly squashed by the bank , Ruark said . 

 " All of a sudden , there 's more risk infrastructure and IT infrastructure , " Ruark added of burdens bank acquisitions imposed on fintechs . " And then they get dissatisfied and do n't want to work there . " 

 This kind of culture shock is common , a KPMG report from March found . 

 " Banks are much larger and more established , heavily regulated , highly bureaucratic , technologically lagging , and focused on shareholders , " the report said . " Fintechs , by contrast , are autonomous , [[lean]] , entrepreneurial , lightly regulated , and technologically advanced . 

 " Given these stark differences , it 's no wonder that culture is constantly cited as a major source of failure for bank - fintech combinations . " 

 UBS is one recent example of the problems that can plague these unions . The Swiss bank grabbed headlines with its planned acquisition of the automated - investing app Wealthfront for $ 1.4 billion in early 2022 . But the deal was called off less than eight months later in a move that revealed internal tensions over the CEO 's push to digitize a 160 - year - old firm soaked in tradition . 

 Jamie Dimon , Chairman and CEO of JPMorgan , has vowed to " spend whatever we have to spend " to win the war with fintechs . MICHEL EULER / POOL / AFP via Getty Images 

 It 's just the latest evidence that banks — despite their deep pockets — are poised to lose their battle with fintechs over talent , technology , and ultimately customers unless they wake up to the fact that they are fighting the wrong fight . The battle is not with up - and - comers like Robinhood and Chime . It 's with themselves and their [[rigid]] , buttoned - down ways , which limit innovation and drive away the tech talent they so desperately want to recruit . 

 Insider spoke with [[more]] than a dozen [[current]] and former bank technologists , executives , consultants , and [[other]] industry pros who had studied or witnessed the battle between banks and fintechs . They all agreed that banks still did n't get it after all these years of throwing money and resources at trying to defeat their fintech foes . The experts pointed to cultural issues at banks — from them not valuing back - office techies enough to being overly bureaucratic in their processes to lacking work flexibility — as being [[core]] to the problem . The only factor weighing against the banks that 's not within their control , the experts said , is the burden of government regulation . 

 If anyone doubts banks ' desperation to beat fintechs , just look to Jamie Dimon , the head of JPMorgan , the US 's largest bank , who has vowed to " spend whatever we have to spend " to win the war with fintechs and emerge triumphant from the " very [[tough]] , brutal competition . " 

 It 's not just Dimon . An analysis of earnings calls and shareholder - conference transcripts on the investment - research platform Sentieo found that among six of the top US banks , the number of times the words " tech " and " digital " were used by executives skyrocketed from just 17 in 2011 to 81 in 2021 . 

 But talking like a tech company and acting like one are two different things . Real transformation ( as we all know from the multibillion - dollar self - help industry ) comes from within . And banks are set to keep spending time , money , and effort on this [[perpetual]] battle until they open their eyes to their internal and cultural shortcomings . 

 " If you 're an engineer and you have a choice of where you want to work , you would rather work in a place where the thing you 're building is directly contributing to the P&L or the alpha of that firm , " said Neal Pawar , a long time Wall Street tech vet who 's the chief operating officer at Qontigo , an investment - data fintech . 

 " In a bank or asset manager , technology is a means to an end , " said Pawar , who previously served as a tech exec at Deutsche Bank , UBS , AQR , and D.E. Shaw . 

 For the past couple of centuries , banks have proved they are not easy to replace . But that has n't stopped disruptors from trying . 

 While banks still rule when it comes to deposits and customers , they 've struggled to keep up with the sleek designs and ease of use made mainstream by fintechs from all angles — payments fintechs like Block and PayPal , digital wealth advisors like Wealthfront and Betterment , digital banks like Chime , and online brokerages like Robinhood . 

 To compete , banks have written fat checks to acquire fintechs — tech , talent , and all . 

 Banks may see a reprieve with the current downturn devastating tech startups , but the jury is still out on whether they will do what it takes to keep tech talent when the economy rebounds and employment opportunities open up . While banks have the money , the smarts , and the willpower to beat fintechs , they are missing one key ingredient : a culture that lets techies thrive . 

 There is still a perception in banks that the tech side is almost second to the business side . Falguni Desai 

 At banks , technologists do n't receive the recognition , or have the decision - making power , they might expect from firms increasingly hanging their futures on the power of their technology and their ability to innovate . Programmers working for big banks report feeling undervalued compared with [[front]] - office investment bankers , traders , and other bankers , people interviewed for this story said . 

 It 's not just being treated as second - class citizens ; it 's being paid like them , too . Banks have historically struggled to keep up with the inflated salaries and equity packages offered by fintechs and Big Tech companies , Insider has previously reported . 

 " There is still a perception in banks that the tech side is almost second to the business side , " said Falguni Desai , a banking and capital - markets strategist at Microsoft who was previously an equities- and [[electronic]] - trading strategist at Credit Suisse . 

 There has been some acknowledgement of this from bank executives . 

 Goldman Sachs , for instance — which has struggled to hang on to developers for its consumer bank , Marcus — is now trying to encourage technologists to " feel like they 're on the front line of the business , " Marco Argenti , Goldman Sachs ' chief information officer , said . 

 David Solomon , Chairman and CEO of Goldman Sachs Photo by Michael Kovac / Getty Images 

 " They do n't want to feel like they 're in the back office , " Argenti said at a forum hosted by The Wall Street Journal [[last]] year , referring to bank engineers . 

 But on Wall Street , old habits die hard , and Goldman has struggled to make Marcus , a [[big]] fintech bet , a success . Despite Wall Street 's increasing reliance on technology , tech is n't the star of its show but a supporting actor . And star programmers would rather work at a place where their efforts get the full spotlight treatment . 

 Technologists can also feel stifled by the work culture of the average bank . Heavy regulatory burdens and risk controls mean pushing back against the tech ethos defined by Mark Zuckerberg 's " move fast and break things " motto . But even when it comes to less - controversial details , like flexible work schedules , many banks have shown an inability to let go and innovate . 

 Since the beginning of the pandemic , Wall Street leaders have been at the helm of a push to get their employees back to their desks . Young bankers and traders learn the trade largely by working closely with more - experienced practitioners , these leaders have said . But the apprenticeship argument does n't exactly apply to technologists , whose work mainly requires them to be on the computer writing code . 

 One JPMorgan tech employee in London told Insider [[last]] year , after the bank called him back to his desk , that he did n't understand why he was expected to sit by himself in the office while every other member of his team was on another continent . It seemed pointless , he said . ( A person close to the bank said this person 's experience was an anomaly and that most of the firm 's technologists worked in the same location as their managers . ) 

 Data indicates that programmers , by and large , want the freedom to be flexible about where they work . In a 2022 survey of software engineers by Terminal , an engineering - talent company , about three - quarters of respondents said they " prefer to work remotely most of the time , " and nearly 70 % said they were more productive when doing so . 

 Being forced back to the office is n't the only issue . 

 Red tape is another source of frustration for fast - moving programmers , KPMG 's research found . Some of that is due to regulation , some to sheer size . Plus , the technology at fintechs is often a lot newer , so it 's easier to change , bolt new products onto , and work on as a developer . 

 " Comparing a Bank of America or a JPMorgan Chase to a small fintech , well , of course , you 're going to see more bureaucracy , more red tape , because it 's several hundred , if not thousands , of times the size of that fintech , " said Michael Roberts , a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania who teaches a course on finance and data science . 

 To be [[sure]] , Wall Street 's embrace of the public cloud , which offers developers ready - to - use software tools and automation , is helping banks strip themselves of legacy tech . 

 Goldman Sachs and Capital One tech execs are using the cloud to improve the overall developer experience . At Wells Fargo , the cloud allowed the bank to launch a mobile app in 10 months , something that would 've taken " multiple years " previously , Ather Williams , the bank 's [[senior]] executive vice president and head of strategy , digital , and innovation , told Insider . 

 " Most programmers just want to write code — they want to code , they want to solve problems , they want a digital - product manager that will launch products . Traditionally , that 's been very difficult in banks , " said Williams , who was hired in late 2020 and leads a team designed to bridge the bank 's tech and business teams . 

 Every time you want to make a change to a system , you 've got to have 19 different people sign off on it . A technologist for a bulge - bracket bank 

 But advancements with the cloud can not completely unshackle banks from 30 - year - old tech and ingrained bureaucratic processes . A technologist who works at one of the nation 's largest banks complained to Insider about a project underway last year aimed at replacing a more than 30 - year - old system . The project plodded along for more than two years without an end in sight , the person said said .

 Recently , Insider spoke to a number of Broadway and off - Broadway experts to ask about proper theater etiquette . Below are eight tips to follow the next time you 're in a Broadway theater . 

 1 . Do n't talk during a performance 

 This might sound like an obvious , no - brainer tip , but it bears emphasizing considering how many people commit this breach of audience conduct . Remember : You are not in your living room where no one can hear you except your spouse or your cat . Other theatergoers have ears and so do the actors . 

 For Broadway League theater critic Scott Harrah , this simple rule is one that he has seen too many people ignore at shows . He finds it mind - boggling . 

 He recalled one notorious incident while reviewing the Broadway musical " War Paint " in 2017 . It involved a young woman sitting in a row in front of him . She was sitting with an entourage of " boisterous " people , he said , talking and laughing obnoxiously . 

 " She was also drinking wine and getting more and more intoxicated , " said Harrah , who 's been reviewing shows for New York newspapers since 2005 . He currently serves as editor and publisher of StageZine.com , a theater news and reviews website . 

 " No one would say a word , " he continued . " Why ? She is an A - list celebrity who has won a Tony Award , but she managed to distract everyone in the theater and ruined the show for many of us . 

 " I wonder if she would have appreciated such behavior when she was working on Broadway a few years earlier ? " 

 2 . Cell phones should be completely turned off 

 You hear that ? Not on vibrate or in airplane mode , where they can still flash and annoy fellow theatergoers , but powered off . As in … off . 

 In 2015 , Broadway grande dame Patti LuPone made headlines when she grabbed a cell phone away from a texting audience member during a performance of " Shows for Days " at Lincoln Center . LuPone did n't break character . 

 " She did n't know what was going on , " LuPone told the New York Times at the time . 

 When the pre - show announcement tells you to turn your phone off , please obey that edict . Otherwise , you may risk the chance of having a very irate diva snatch away your iPhone . 

 3 . Do n't block the aisle during intermission or after the show 

 When the show ends and the curtain call is over , it 's common courtesy and good etiquette to grab your things and exit the aisle quickly so everyone can get out . This also means not bringing your shopping bags with you . 

 Robin Rothstein , a playwright and former director of operations at touring - show producer Broadway Across America , told Insider : " The Broadway theaters are old and seats are small . Do n't go shopping at Bloomingdale 's before you go to the theater . People need to realize most of the theaters are not new and require legroom . " 

 4 . Never record video or take photos during a show 

 " It is the ultimate sign of disrespect in the theater , " said off - Broadway performer Jenna Nicole Schoen , whose credits include " Wicked , " " Jersey Boys , " and " A Chorus Line . " " It is very uncomfortable for everyone when you are reminded not to record , especially if the rules are already established . " 

 One of the most infamous incidents involving this infraction was when the late acting great Katharine Hepburn interrupted a 1982 Broadway - bound performance of " West Side Waltz " in Boston to yell at a woman who had , contrary to theater rules , taken a flash photograph of Hepburn in action . The woman was then kicked out of the theater and the performance resumed . 

 5 . Make sure you clap at the end of a musical number — not during it 

 Showing appreciation for a performer by clapping is excellent theater etiquette — but not in the middle of a song . Not only does it qualify as spectacularly bad timing , but it 's distracting to the performers and fellow audience members . 

 Devin E. Haqq , an actor who has appeared off - Broadway with theater companies ranging from the Barrow Group to the Epic Theatre Ensemble , told Insider he recently witnessed a variation of this faux pas while watching a performance of " Springsteen on Broadway . " 

 During the show , he said , an audience member was the only one to clap in the middle of an upbeat ballad — and as a result , was ejected from the theater . Haqq said in speaking to the audience afterward , Springsteen called this gaffe the " bane " of his existence . 

 6 . Do n't wear a sweatsuit or cut - offs 

 This might be counterintuitive to some , since Broadway does n't have a dress code . But if you have spent a great deal of money on a ticket and parking , why would you go to a theater looking like you just crawled out of bed ? 

 As a performer , Schoen appreciates when audience members are dapper and well - groomed . 

 " This one is a tradition that I love and really appreciate , " she said . " When I am heading into the show and I see people a little spruced up , it gets me really excited to perform for them and give them a [[special]] night . It shows a lot of respect and class . " 

 7 . Keep your masks on while you 're in the theater 

 This is necessary to protect the actors on stage and your fellow audience members , said Broadway producer Dan Stone , whose credits include " Dear Evan Hansen " and " Moulin Rouge . " 

 " Theaters do not want to run the risk of having to close down due to positive COVID-19 cases , " he said . " They 've worked too hard to bring live theater back . " 

 8 . Arrive early 

 Being late is jarring because it interrupts the flow of production and movement of a show , even if you 're being escorted by an usher to your seat . 

 But it 's not enough to be on time . You have to be early these days , said Charlene Speyerer , a veteran Broadway stage manager who is currently providing COVID-19 safety training to shows like " Caroline or Change " and " Mrs. Doubtfire . " 

 Speyerer said during this ongoing pandemic , when Broadway theatergoers must show their vaccination cards and ID upon checking in , it 's crucial to get to the theater early to move through the line in an efficient manner . 

 " Use the restroom without a long line , " she said . " Then , relax in your seat with your mask on as you read the playbill and celebrate all of the artists who have joyfully returned to work after an 18 - month hiatus . " 

 Amen ! Now that you know the eight rules of proper Broadway etiquette , buy a ticket and enjoy a show .
